It can help improve infrastructure resilience with POWER9\nhigh-end systems engineered to deliver the highest level of IBM Power\nArchitecture reliability, availability, and serviceability.\nThe IBM Power System E980 server, is the ideal foundation for a\nprivate cloud infrastructure, able to power the large-scale,\nmission-critical applications enterprises need to transform data into a\ncompetitive advantage.  Each Power E980 comes tailored to a client's\nunique requirements and ready to deploy--with enterprise-class\nsecurity and efficient, built-in IBM PowerVM virtualization.\nWith built-in virtualization and an ecosystem of open cloud\nsolutions, you can cloud-enable your applications without migration\nand build a cloud that handles the most data-intensive workloads on\nearth.\nEnable large-scale consolidation of older, under-utilized servers\nonto an ultra-efficient POWER9 high-end system with high levels of\nutilization and resource sharing to concurrently support AIX, IBM i,\nand Linux applications.\nEnable rapid service delivery with built-in virtualization and CoD\nfor processors and memory to help provide seamless, nondisruptive\ngrowth and increased flexibility for multiple systems in an enterprise\nprivate cloud.\nBy default, its Power Management mode is set to Max Performance.\nThis mode can dynamically optimize the processor frequency at any\ngiven time based on CPU utilization and operating environmental\nconditions.  For a description of this feature and other power\nmanagement options available for this server, see the\nIBM EnergyScale for POWER9 Processor-Based Systems\nwebsite.\nEach POWER9 processor single chip module (SCM) contains two memory\ncontrollers. Four 6-core typical 3.58 - 3.90 GHz (max) or four 8-core\ntypical 3.9 - 4.0 GHz (max) or four 10-core typical 3.7 - 3.9 GHz (max)\nor four 11-core typical 3.58 - 3.9 GHz (max) or four 12-core typical 3.55\n- 3.9 GHz (max) are used in each system node, providing 24 cores to a\n96-core system (max)(#EFP0) or 32 cores to a 128-core system (max)(#EFP1)\nor 40 cores to a 160-core system (max)(#EFP2) or 44-core to a 176-core\nsystem (max)(#EFP4) or 48 cores to a 192-core system (max) (#EFP3). As\nfew as eight cores in the system can be activated or up to 100% of the\ncores in the system can be activated. Incrementing one core at a time is\navailable through built-in Capacity Upgrade on Demand (CUoD) functions to\nthe full capacity of the system.\nThe System Control Unit provides redundant Flexible Service\nProcessors (FSPs), the Operator Panel, and the System Vital Product\n(VPD).  And optional external DVD can be attached with a USB cable.\nIBM custom DIMMs (CDIMMs) are high-performance, high-reliability,\nhigh-function memory cards that contain L4 cache buffer, and 1600 MHz\nDRAM memory.\nIBM Power System E980 CDIMMs are available as 128 GB (#EF20), 256\nGB (#EF21), 512 GB (#EF22), 1024 GB (#EF23), and 2048 GB (#EF24)\nmemory features.  Each memory feature provides four CDIMMs.  Each\nsystem node has 32 CDIMM slots that support a maximum of 8 memory\nfeatures.  Using 2048 GB CDIMM features yields a maximum of 16 TB per\nnode.  A two-node system has a maximum of 16 memory features and 32\nTB.  A four-node system has a maximum of 64 TB capacity.  Minimum\nmemory activations of 50% of the installed capacity are required.\nThe 19-inch PCIe 4U I/O Expansion Drawer (#EMX0) provides 12 slots\nto hold PCIe adapters that cannot be placed into a system node.  Up to\nfour PCIe I/O expansion drawers can be attached per system node.  For\nexample, a two-node system can have a maximum of eight PCIe I/O\nexpansion drawers for a total of eighty-six PCIe slots in the I/O\ndrawers with no PCIe slots in the system node.\nDirect attached storage is supported with the EXP24SX SFF Gen2-bay\nDrawer (#ESLS), an expansion drawer with twenty-four 2.5-inch\nform-factor SAS bays.\nWith Power Enterprise Pools, IBM continues to enhance the ability\nto freely move Mobile Processor and Mobile Memory activations from one\nsystem to another system in the same pool, without the need for IBM\ninvolvement.  This capability enables the movement of resources not\nonly between Power E980 systems, but also between IBM Power System\nE980 servers and previous generation E870, E870C, E880, and E880C\nsystems, resulting in unsurpassed flexibility for workload balancing\nand system maintenance. For more\ninformation, visit\nIBM Cloud Management Console\nwebsite.\nIBM Power System E980 server POWER9 hardware components\nSix, eight, ten, eleven, or twelve core processors\nUp to 192 POWER9 processor cores in one to four systems nodes; up\nto 64 TB of 1600 MHz, DDR4 DRAM memory, and eight PCIe G4 x16 I/O\nexpansion slots per system node enclosure, with a maximum of 32 per\nsystem\nRedundant Clocking in each system node\nFour NVMe drive bays per system node for boot purposes\nIntegrated USB ports\nSystem control unit, providing redundant system master Flexible\nService Processor (FSP) and support for the Op Panel, the system VPD,\nand external attached DVD\n19-inch PCIe Gen3 4U I/O expansion drawer and PCIe FanOut modules,\nsupporting a maximum of 48 PCIe slots (2 I/O expansion drawers per\nnode in the September GA, which has maximum of 2 nodes)\n19-inch PCIe Gen3 4U I/O expansion drawer and PCIe FanOut modules,\nsupporting a maximum of 192 PCIe slots (4 I/O expansion drawers per\nnode in the November GA, which has a maximum of 4 nodes)\nPCIe Gen1, Gen2, Gen3, and Gen4 adapter cards, supported in the\nsystem node and PCIe Gen1, Gen2, Gen3 and Gen4 adapter cards,\nsupported in I/O expansion drawer\nEXP24SX SFF Drawer with twenty-four 2.5-inch form-factor SAS bays\nDynamic LPAR support for adjusting workload placement of processor\nand memory resources\nRespond more rapidly and seamlessly to changing business\nrequirements and growth with Capacity on Demand (CoD) for processors\nand memory\nActive Memory Expansion that is optimized onto the processor chip\nPower Enterprise Pools that support unsurpassed enterprise\nflexibility for workload balancing and system maintenance\nModel abstract 9080-M9S\nThe IBM 9080 Model M9S is a Power E980 with POWER9 system node that\nuses 6-core, 8-core, 10-core, 11-core or 12-core symmetric\nmultiprocessing (SMP) processor chips with 512 KB of L2 and 10 MB of\nL3 cache per core, DDR3 or DDR4 CDIMM memory, dual memory controllers,\nand an industry-standard PCIe I/O bus that is designed to use 32 lanes\norganized in two sets of x16.  The two primary system building blocks\nare one system control unit and one or more system nodes.  Additional\nI/O support is provided with a 19-inch PCIe I/O expansion drawer and\nan EXP24S SFF expansion drawer.  The processors, memory, and base I/O\nare packaged within the system nodes.  The system nodes are rack\nbased.\nHighlights\nThe IBM Power Systems E980 server offers the next generation of IBM\nPower Systems servers with POWER9 technology-based processors.  It is\nbuilt with innovations that can help deliver security and reliability\nfor the data-intensive workloads of today's enterprises.  POWER9\ntechnology is designed from the ground up for data-intensive workloads\nlike databases and analytics.  The Power System E980 server:\nIncludes high throughput, performance, and scalability\nHelps enable large-scale consolidation of older, underutilized\nservers\nHelps improve infrastructure resilience\nEnables rapid service delivery\nThe IBM Power System E980 server provides the underlying POWER9\nhardware components:\nThe most powerful and scalable server in the IBM Power Systems\nportfolio:\nUp to 192 POWER9 technology-based processor cores\nUp to 64 TB memory\nUp to 32 PCIe Gen4 x16 slots in system nodes\nUp to 192 PCIe Gen3 slots with expansion drawers\nUp to over 4,000 directly attached SAS disks or solid-state drives\n(SSDs)\nUp to 1,000 VMs (LPARs) per system\nSystem control unit, providing redundant system master Flexible\nService Processor (FSP)\nSupport for IBM AIX, IBM i, and Linux environments\nCapacity on demand (CoD) processor and memory options\nModel upgrades from IBM POWER8\nPower Enterprise Pools, supporting unsurpassed enterprise\nflexibility for workload balancing and system maintenance\nDescription\nThe IBM Power System E980 server is a large-scale SMP system that\ndelivers high performance, scalability, reliability, availability, and\nserviceability with great virtualization capability for larger cloud\nenvironments.  The IBM Power System E980 server uses modular building\nblocks called\nsystem nodes\n. The E980 can have one or two\nsystem nodes.\nThe Power System E980 server will support three and four systems\nnodes by November 16, 2018.\nSummary of features\nThe following features are available on the IBM Power System E980\nserver:\nOne or two 5U system nodes (in November, one to four)\nOne 2U system control unit\nOne to four processor features per system with four single-chip\nmodules (SCMs) per feature:\nTypical 3.9 - 4.0 GHz, 32-core POWER9 processor (#EFP1)\nTypical 3.7 - 3.9 GHz, 40-core POWER9 processor (#EFP2)\nTypical 3.58 - 3.9 GHz, 44-core POWER9 processor (#EFP4)\nTypical 3.55 - 3.9 GHz, 48-core POWER9 processor (#EFP3)\nTypical 3.58 - 3.90 GHz, 24-core POWER9 processor (#EFP0).\nCoD processor core activation features available on a per-core\nbasis\n32 CDIMM slots per system node\nDDR4 1600 MHz CDIMM memory cards:\n128 GB (4 x 32 GB), (#EF20)\n256 GB (4 x 64 GB), (#EF21)\n512 GB (4 x 128 GB), (#EF22)\n1024 GB (4 x 256 GB), (#EF23)\n2048 GB (4 x 512 GB), (#EF24)\nCoD memory activation features include:\n1 GB (static) Memory Activations (#EMAT)\n100 GB (static) Memory Activations (#EMAU)\n100 GB Mobile Memory Activations (#EMAV)\n100 GB Mobile Enabled Memory Activations (#EMAD)\n512 GB Memory Activations for Linux (#ELMD)\nPlus activations for a few specific bundle scenarios\nActive Memory Expansion, optimized onto the processor chip (#EM89)\nEight PCIe Gen4 x16 I/O low-profile expansion slots per system\nnode (maximum 32 in a 4-node system)\nOne USB port to support external attached DVD\nRedundant hot-swap AC power supplies in each system node drawer\nTwo HMC ports in the system control unit\nOptional PCIe I/O Expansion Drawer with PCIe slots:\nZero to two drawers per system node drawer (#EMX0).\nEach I/O drawer holds one or two 6-slot PCIe Fan-out Modules\n(#EMXG).\nEach Fan-out Module attaches to the system node through a PCIe\nOptical Cable Adapter (#EJ07).\nSystem nodes\nEach 5 EIA or 5U system node of the system has four air-cooled SCMs\noptimized for performance and scalability. The E980 SCMs can have eight,\nten, eleven, or twelve POWER9 cores running at up to 4.0 GHz and\nsimultaneous multithreading executing up to eight threads per core. Each\nSCM has dual memory controllers to support up to 128 MB off-chip eDRAM L4\ncache to deliver up to 230 GBps of peak memory bandwidth or 920 GBps per\nnode. Using PCIe Gen4 I/O controllers, which are also integrated onto\neach SCM to further reduce latency, up to 545 GBps peak I/O bandwidth is\navailable per node. Thus a Power E980 system bandwidth can help provide\nmaximum processor performance , enabling applications to run faster and\nbe more responsive.\nEach system node has 32 CDIMM slots and can support up to 16 TB of\nDDR4 memory.  Thus, a four-node server can have up to 64 TB of memory.\nThe system node has four internal NVMe U.2 (2.5\" 7mm form factor)\nSSDs.  Each SSD is driven from a x4 PCIe connection.  Each system node\nhas eight PCIe slots, which are all x16, low profile.  Thus, a\nfour-node server can have up to 32 PCIe slots.  PCIe expansion units can\noptionally expand the number of PCIe slots on the server.\nA system node is ordered using a processor feature.  Each processor\nfeature will deliver a set of four identical SCMs in one system node.\nAll processor features in the system must be identical.  Cable\nfeatures are required to connect system node drawers to the system\ncontrol unit and to other system nodes.\nProcessor core activations\nEach IM Power System E980 server requires a minimum of eight\npermanent processor core activations, using either static activations\nor Linux on Power activations.  This minimum is per system, not per\nnode.  The rest of the cores can be permanently or temporary activated\nor remain inactive (dark) until needed.  The activations are not\nspecific to hardware cores or SCMs or nodes.  They are known to the\nsystem as a total number of activations of different types and used or\nassigned by the Power hypervisor appropriately.\nA variety of activations fit different usage and pricing options.\nStatic activations are permanent and support any type of application\nenvironment on this server.  Mobile activations are ordered against a\nspecific server, but can be moved to any server within the Power\nEnterprise Pool and can support any type of application.\nMobile-enabled activations are technically static, but can be\nconverted to mobile at no charge when logistically or administratively\neligible.  Linux on Power activations can only run Linux workloads.\nTemporary activations are used for CoD - Elastic, Utility, and Trial\noptions.\n48-core (#EFP3)    44-core (#EFP4)   40-core (#EFP2)   32-core (#EFP1)\n------------------ ----------------- ----------------- -----------------\n1-core static      1-core static     1-core static     1-core static\nactivation (#EFPC) activation        activation        activation\n                   (#EFP9)           (#EFPB)           (#EFPA)\n1-core             1-core            1-core            1-core\nmobile-enabled     mobile-enabled    mobile-enabled    mobile-enabled\nactivation (#EFPG) activation        activation        activation\n                   (#EFPN)           (#EFPF)           (#EFPE)\n1-core Power Linux 1-core Power      1-core Power      1-core Power\n(#ELBM)            Linux (#ELBQ)     Linux (#ELBL)     Linux (#ELBK)\n \n24-core (#EFP0)\n----------------\n1-core static\nactivation\n(#EFPQ)\n1-core\nmobile-enabled\nactivation\n(#EFPR)\n1-core Power\nLinux (#ELBS)\nSystem control unit\nThe 2U system control unit provides redundant system master\nFlexible Service Processor (FSP).  Additionally, it contains the\nOperator Panel, the System VPD, and external attached DVD.  One system\ncontrol unit is required for each server.  A unique feature number is\nnot used to order the system control unit.  One is shipped with each\nE980 server.  Two service processors (FSPs) in the system control unit\nare ordered using two EFFP features.  All system nodes connect to the\nsystem control unit using the cable features EFCA, EFCB, EFCC, and\nEFCD.\nThe system control unit is powered from the system nodes.  UPIC\ncables provide redundant power to the system control unit.  In a\nsingle node system, two UPIC cables are attached to system node 1.  In\na 2-node, 3-node, or 4-node system, one UPIC cable attaches to system\nnode 1 and one UPIC cable attaches to system node 2.  They are ordered\nwith features EFCA.  Only one UPIC cable is enough to power the system\ncontrol unit, and the others are in place for redundancy.\nIf the optional DVD feature EUA5 is ordered, it attaches to the native\nUSB ports in the system (one in the front of the System Control Unit or\nthe several in the rear of nodes 1 and 2).\nMemory\nIBM-custom DIMMs (CDIMMs) are extremely high-performance,\nhigh-reliability, high-function memory cards that contain L4 cache,\nintelligence, and 1600 MHz DRAM memory.  Both DDR3 and DDR4 technology\nis employed and both provide the same 1600 MHz performance.  CDIMMs\nare placed in CDIMM slots in the system node.\nEach system node has 32 memory CDIMM slots, and at least half of\nthe memory slots are always physically filled.  Eight CDIMM slots are\nlocal to each of the four SCMs in the server, but SCMs and their cores\nhave access to all the other memory in the server.  At least half of\nthe eight memory slots for each SCM must physically be filled.  When\nfilling the other four memory slots in the SCM, a quantity of four\nCDIMMs must be used.  Thus, the CDIMM slots of the SCMs are either 50%\nor 100% filled.  The system node (four SCMs) CDIMM slots can have 16,\n20, 24, 28, or 32 CDIMMs physically installed (quad plugging rules).\nTo assist with the quad plugging rules above, four CDIMMs are\nordered using one memory feature number.  Select from 128 GB feature\nEF20 (4 x 32 DDR4), 256 GB feature EF21 (4 x 64 DDR4), 512 GB feature\nEF22 (4 x 128 DDR4), 1024 GB feature EF23 (4 x 256 DDR4), or 2048 GB\nfeature EF24 (4 x 512 DDR4).\nAll CDIMMs must be identical on the same SCM so if using eight\nCDIMMs, both memory features on an SCM must be identical.  A different\nSCM in the same system node can use a different memory feature.  For\nexample, one system node could technically use 128 GB, 256 GB, 512 GB,\n1024 GB, and 2048 GB memory features.  Note that DDR3 and DDR4 memory\ncannot be mixed on the same system node.\nTo provide more flexible pricing, memory activations are ordered\nseparately from the physical memory and can be permanent or temporary.\nActivation features can be used on DDR4 memory features and used on\nany size memory feature.  Activations are not specific to a CDIMM, but\nare known as a total quantity to the server.  The Power hypervisor\ndetermines what physical memory to use.\nMemory activation features are:\n1 GB Memory Activation (#EMAT) (static)\n100 GB Memory Activations (#EMAU) (static)\n100 GB Mobile Memory Activations (#EMAV)\n100 GB Mobile Enabled Memory Activations (#EMAD) (technically\nstatic, but no charge to convert to mobile)\n512 GB Memory Activations for Power Linux (#ELMD)\n8 TB activations (#EMBA) ordered with 8 TB memory using feature\nEM8Y CDIMMs\n4 TB activations (#EMB7) ordered with 4 TB memory using the\nfeature EMB6 package\nA minimum of 50% of the total physical memory capacity of a server\nmust have permanent memory activations ordered for that server.  For\nexample, a server with a total of 8 TB of physical memory must have at\nleast 4 TB of permanent memory activations ordered for that server.\nThese activations can be static, mobile-enabled, mobile, or Linux on\nPower.  At least 25% must be static activations or Linux on Power\nactivations.  For example, a server with a total of 8 TB physical\nmemory must have at least 2 TB of static activations or Linux on Power\nactivations.  The 50% minimum cannot be fulfilled using mobile\nactivations ordered on a different server.\nThe minimum activations ordered with MES orders of additional\nphysical memory features will depend on the existing total installed\nphysical memory capacity and the existing total installed memory\nactivation features.  If you already have installed more than 50%\nactivations for your existing system, then you can order less than 50%\nactivations for the MES ordered memory.  The resulting configuration\nafter the MES order of physical memory and any MES activations must\nmeet the same 50% and 25% minimum rules above.\nFor the best possible performance, it is generally recommended that\nmemory be installed evenly across all system node drawers and all SCMs\nin the system.  Balancing memory across the installed system planar\ncards enables memory access in a consistent manner and typically\nresults in better performance for your configuration.\nThough maximum memory bandwidth is achieved by filling all the\nmemory slots, plans for future memory additions should be taken into\naccount when deciding which memory feature size to use at the time of\ninitial system order.\nIBM Active Memory Expansion (AME) is an option that can increase\nthe effective memory capacity of the system.  See the AME information\nlater in this section.\nSystem node PCIe slots\nEach system node enclosure provides excellent configuration\nflexibility and expandability with eight half-length, low-profile\n(half-high) x16 PCIe Gen4 slots.  The slots are labeled C1 through C8.\nThese PCIe slots can be used for either low-profile PCIe adapters\nor for attaching a PCIe I/O drawer.\nA blind swap cassette (BSC) is used to house the low-profile\nadapters that go into these slots.  The server is shipped with a full\nset of BSCs, even if the BSCs are empty.  A feature number to order\nadditional low-profile BSCs is not required or announced.\nIf additional PCIe slots beyond the system node slots are\nrequired, a system node x16 slot is used to attach a six-slot\nexpansion module in the I/O drawer.  An I/O drawer holds two expansion\nmodules that are attached to any two x16 PCIe slots in the same system\nnode or in different system nodes.\nPCIe Gen1, Gen2, Gen3, and Gen4 adapter cards are supported in\nthese Gen4 slots.  The set of PCIe adapters that are supported is\nfound in the Sales Manual, identified by feature number.\nConcurrent repair and add/removal of PCIe adapter cards is done by\nHMC-guided menus or by operating system support utilities.\nThe system nodes sense which IBM PCIe adapters are installed in\ntheir PCIe slots; and if an adapter requires higher levels of cooling,\nthey automatically speed up the fans to increase airflow across the\nPCIe adapters.\nEach PCIe slot in the system node supports CAPI adapters.\nPCIe I/O Expansion Drawer\nThe 19-inch PCIe 4U I/O Expansion Drawer (#EMX0) provides slots to\nhold PCIe adapters that cannot be placed into a system node.  The PCIe\nI/O Expansion Drawer (#EMX0) and two PCIe FanOut Modules (#EMXG)\nprovide 12 PCIe I/O full-length, full-height slots.  One FanOut Module\nprovides six PCIe slots labeled C1 through C6.  The C1 and C4 are x16\nslots, and C2, C3, C5, and C6 are x8 slots.\nPCIe Gen1, Gen2, Gen3, and Gen4 and full-high adapter cards are\nsupported.  The set of full-high PCIe adapters that are supported is\nfound in the Sales Manual, identified by feature number.  See the PCI\nAdapter Placement manual for the 9080-M9S for details and rules\nassociated with specific adapters supported and their supported\nplacement in x8 or x16 slots.\nUp to four PCIe I/O drawers per node can be attached to the IBM\nPower System E980 server.  Using two 6-slot fan-out modules per drawer\nprovides a maximum of 48 PCIe slots per system node.  With 2 system\nnodes, up to 96 PCIe slots (8 I/O drawers) are supported.  With a\n4-node Power E980 server, up to 192 PCIe slots (16 I/O drawers) are\nsupported.\nAdditional PCIe I/O drawer configuration flexibility is provided to\nthe IBM Power System E980 servers.  Zero, one, two, three, or four\nPCIe I/O drawers can be attached per system node.  As an alternative,\na \"half\" drawer that consists of just one PCIe fan-out module in the\nI/O drawer is also supported, enabling a lower-cost configuration if\nfewer PCIe slots are required.  Thus, a system node supports the\nfollowing half drawer options:  one half drawer, two half drawers,\nthree half drawers, or four half drawers.  Because there is a maximum\nof four feature EMX0 drawers per node, a single system node cannot\nhave more than four half drawers.  A server with more system nodes can\nsupport more half drawers up to four per node.  A system can also mix\nhalf drawers and full PCIe I/O drawers.  The maximum of four PCIe\ndrawers per system node applies whether a full or half PCIe drawer.\nPCIe drawers can be concurrently added to the server at a later\ntime.  The drawer being added can have either one or two fan-out\nmodules.  Note that adding a second fan-out module to a half-full\ndrawer does require schedule downtime.\nPCIe I/O Drawer attachment and cabling\nA PCIe X16 to Optical CXP converter adapter (#EJ07) and 2.0 M\n(#ECC6), 10.0 M (#ECC8), or 20 M (#ECC9) CXP 16X Active Optical cables\n(AOC) connect the system node to a PCIe FanOut module in the I/O\nexpansion drawer.  One ECC6, ECC8, or ECC9 feature ships two AOC\ncables from IBM.\nThe two AOC cables connect to two CXP ports on the fan-out module\nand to two CXP ports on the feature EJ07 adapter.  The top port of the\nfan-out module must be cabled to the top port of the feature EJ07\nport.  Likewise, the bottom two ports must be cabled together.\nIt is recommended but not required that one I/O drawer be attached\nto two different system nodes in the same server (one drawer module\nattached to one system node and the other drawer module attached to a\ndifferent system node).  This can help provide cabling for higher\navailability configurations.\nIt is generally recommended that any attached PCIe I/O Expansion\nDrawer be located in the same rack as the POWER9 server for ease of\nservice, but expansion drawers can be installed in separate racks if\nthe application or other rack content requires it.  If you are\nattaching a large number of cables, such as SAS cables or CAT5/CAT6\nEthernet cables, to a PCIe I/O drawer, then it is generally better to\nplace that feature EMX0 drawer in a separate rack for better cable\nmanagement.\nLimitation:\nWhen this cable is ordered with a system in\na rack specifying IBM Plant integration, IBM Manufacturing will ship\nSAS cables longer than 3 meters in a separate box and not attempt to\nplace the cable in the rack.  This is because the longer SAS cable is\nprobably used to attach to an EXP24S drawer in a different rack.\nConcurrent repair and add/removal of PCIe adapter cards is done by\nHMC-guided menus or by operating system support utilities.\nA blind swap cassette is used to house the full-high adapters that\ngo into these slots.  The BSC is the same BSC as used with 12X\nattached I/O drawers (#5802, #5803, #5877, #5873) of the previous\ngeneration server.  The drawer is shipped with a full set of BSCs,\neven if the BSCs are empty.  A feature to order additional full-high\nBSCs is not required or announced.\nA maximum of 16 EXP24s Drawers is needed per PCIe Drawer (#EMX0)\nto enable SAS cables to be properly handled by the feature EMX0 cable\nmanagement bracket.\nA BSC is used to house the full-high adapters that go into the\nfan-out module slots.  The BSC is the same BSC as used with the 12X\nattached I/O drawers (#5802, #5803, #5877, #5873) of the previous\ngeneration server and is often referred to as a\ncassette\n.\nThe drawer is shipped with a full set of BSCs, even if the BSCs are\nempty.  A feature number to order additional full-high BSC is not\nrequired or announced.\nEXP24SX disk/SSD drawer\nDirect attached storage is supported with the EXP24SX SFF Gen2-bay\nDrawer (#ESLS), an expansion drawer with twenty-four 2.5-inch form-\nfactor SAS bays.\nThe Power E980 server supports up to 4,032 drives with a maximum\nof 168 EXP24SX drawers.  The maximum of 16 EXP24SX drawers per PCIe\nI/O drawer due to cabling considerations remains unchanged.\nThe EXP24SX SFF Gen2-bay Drawer (#ESLS) is an expansion drawer\nwith twenty-four 2.5-inch form-factor SAS bays.  Slot filler panels\nare included for empty bays when initially shipped.  The EXP24SX\nsupports up to 24 hot-swap SFF-2 SAS HDDs or SSDs.  It uses only 2 EIA\nof space in a 19-inch rack.  The EXP24SX includes redundant AC power\nsupplies and uses two power cords.\nWith AIX, Linux, and VIOS, you can order the EXP24SX with four\nsets of six bays, two sets of 12 bays, or one set of 24 bays (mode 4,\n2, or 1).  With IBM i, you can order the EXP24SX as one set of 24 bays\n(mode 1).  Mode setting is done by IBM Manufacturing, and there is no\noption provided to change the mode after it is shipped from IBM.\nImportant:  When changing modes, a skilled, technically qualified\nperson should follow the special documented procedures.  Improperly\nchanging modes can potentially destroy existing RAID sets, prevent\naccess to existing data, or allow other partitions to access another\npartition's existing data.  Hire an expert to assist if you are not\nfamiliar with this type of reconfiguration work.\nThe EXP24SX SAS ports are attached to a SAS PCIe adapter or pair\nof adapters using SAS YO or X cables.\nTo maximize configuration flexibility and space utilization, the\nsystem node does not have integrated SAS bays or integrated SAS\ncontrollers.  PCIe adapters and the EXP24SX can be used to provide\ndirect access storage.\nTo further reduce possible single points of failure, EXP24SX\nconfiguration rules consistent with previous IBM Power Systems servers\nare used.  IBM i configurations require the drives to be protected\n(RAID or mirroring).  Protecting the drives is highly recommended, but\nnot required for other operating systems.  All Power operating system\nenvironments that are using SAS adapters with write cache require the\ncache to be protected by using pairs of adapters.\nIt is recommended for SAS cabling ease that the EXP24SX drawer be\nlocated in the same rack in which the PCIe adapter is located.  Note,\nhowever, it is often a good availability practice to split a SAS\nadapter pair across two PCIe drawers/nodes for availability and that\nmay make the SAS cabling ease recommendation difficult or impossible\nto implement.\nHDDs and SSDs that were previously located in POWER8 system units\nor in feature 5802 or 5803 12X-attached I/O drawers (SFF-1 bays) can\nbe \"re-trayed\" and placed in EXP24S drawers.  See feature conversions\npreviously announced on the POWER8 servers.  Ordering a conversion\nships an SFF-2 tray or carriage onto which the client can place their\nexisting drive after removing it from the existing SFF-1\ntray/carriage.  The order also changes the feature number so that IBM\nconfiguration tools can better interpret what is required.\nA maximum of 16 EXP24SX Drawers is needed per PCIe Drawer (#EMX0)\nto enable SAS cables to be properly handled by the feature EMX0 cable\nmanagement bracket.\nA maximum of 999 SSDs can be ordered within a single order\n(initial or MES) of the system.\nDVD and boot devices\nA device capable of reading a DVD may be attached to the system and\navailable to perform operating system installation, maintenance,\nproblem determination, and service actions such as maintaining system\nfirmware and I/O microcode at their latest levels.  In addition, the\nsystem must be attached to a network with software such as AIX NIM\nserver or Linux Install Manager configured to perform these functions:\nDisk or SSD located in an EXP24S drawer attached to a PCIe adapter\nA network through LAN adapters\nA SAN attached to Fibre Channel or Fibre Channel over Ethernet\nadapters and indicated to the server by the 0837 specify feature\nAssuming option 1 above, the minimum system configuration requires\nat least one SAS disk drive in the system for AIX and Linux and two\nfor IBM i. In\na 2-node, 3-node, or 4-node system, one UPIC cable attaches to system\nnode 1 and one UPIC cable attaches to system node 2.  They are ordered\nwith features EFCA.  Only one UPIC cable is enough to power the system\ncontrol unit, and the other is in place for redundancy.\nConcurrent maintenance or Hot-plug options\nThe following options are maintenance or hot-plug capable:\nEXP24S SAS Storage enclosure drawer.\nDrives in the EXP24S Storage enclosure drawer.\nNVMe U.2 drives.\nPCI extender cards, Optical PCIe Link IO Expansion Card.\nPCIe I/O adapters.\nPCIe I/O drawers.\nPCIe to USB Conversion card.\nSMP cables. This can enable a partition to do\nsignificantly more work or support more users with the same physical\namount of memory.  Similarly, it can enable a server to run more\npartitions and do more work for the same physical amount of memory.\nActive Memory Expansion uses CPU resource to compress/decompress\nthe memory contents.  The trade-off of memory capacity for processor\ncycles can be an excellent choice, but the degree of expansion varies\non how compressible the memory content is.  It also depends on having\nadequate spare CPU capacity available for this\ncompression/decompression.\nThe IBM Power System E980 server includes a hardware accelerator\ndesigned to boost Active Memory Expansion efficiency and uses less\nPOWER core resource.  You have a great deal of control over Active\nMemory Expansion usage.  Each individual AIX partition can turn on or\nturn off Active Memory Expansion.  Control parameters set the amount\nof expansion desired in each partition to help control the amount of\nCPU used by the Active Memory Expansion function.  An IPL is required\nfor the specific partition that is turning memory expansion.  When\nturned on, monitoring capabilities are available in standard AIX\nperformance tools such as lparstat, vmstat, topas, and svmon.\nA planning tool is included with AIX, enabling you to sample actual\nworkloads and estimate both how expandable the partition's memory is\nand how much CPU resource is needed.  Any IBM Power Systems model can\nrun the planning tool.  In addition, a one-time, 60-day trial of\nActive Memory Expansion is available to enable more exact memory\nexpansion and CPU measurements.  You can request the trial using the\nCapacity on Demand\nweb page.\nActive Memory Expansion is enabled by chargeable hardware feature\nEM89, which can be ordered with the initial order of the system or as\nan MES order.  A software key is provided when the enablement feature\nis ordered, which is applied to the system node.  An IPL is not\nrequired to enable the system node.  The key is specific to an\nindividual system and is permanent.  It cannot be moved to a different\nserver.\nThe additional CPU resource used to expand memory is part of the\nCPU resource assigned to the AIX partition running Active Memory\nExpansion.  Normal licensing requirements apply.\nActive Memory Mirroring\nThe IBM Power System E980 server offers the Active Memory Mirroring\nfor Hypervisor feature, which is designed to prevent a system outage\nin the event of an uncorrectable error in memory being used by the\nsystem hypervisor.\nIBM i operating system\nFor clients loading the IBM i operating system, the four-digit\nnumeric QPRCFEAT value is generally the same as the four-digit numeric\nfeature number for the processors used in the system. During the design\nand development process, subsystems go through rigorous verification\nand integration testing processes.  During system manufacturing,\nsystems go through a thorough testing process ensure product quality.\nPower E980 system RAS\nThe Power E980 server comes with dual line cord redundancy along\nwith n+1 power supply redundancy and n+1 fan rotor redundancy.  Power\nsupplies and fans are concurrently maintainable.\nThe system service processor is redundant with a dynamic failover\ncapability.  Each system node has dual processor clock logic with a\ndynamic failover capability.\nConcurrent maintenance of the real-time clock battery and the\noperator panel is also provided.\nThe voltage regulators supplying the DIMM risers and certain other\nmiscellaneous functions are pluggable and supply both a redundant and\nspare output.\nMemory subsystem RAS\nThe memory has error detection and correction circuity that can\nmark a memory module as faulty to allow for substitution of a spare\nmemory module.  Both x4 and x8 CDIMMS provide spare memory modules.\nMutual surveillance\nThe service processor monitors the operation of the firmware during\nthe boot process and also monitors the hypervisor for termination.\nThe hypervisor monitors the service processor and reports a service\nreference code when it detects surveillance loss.  In the IBM PowerVM\nenvironment, it will perform a reset/reload if it detects the loss of\nthe service processor.\nEnvironmental monitoring functions\nThe IBM Power Systems family does ambient and over temperature\nmonitoring and reporting.\nPOWER9 processor functions\nAs in POWER8, the POWER9 processor has the ability to do processor\ninstruction retry for some transient errors and provide core-contained\ncheckstops for certain solid faults.\nCache availability\nThe L2 and L3 caches in the POWER9 processor in the memory buffer\nchip are protected with double-bit detect, single-bit correct error\ndetection code (ECC).  In addition, a threshold of correctable errors\ndetected on cache lines can result in the data in the cache lines\nbeing purged and the cache lines removed from further operation\nwithout requiring a reboot in the PowerVM environment.\nModified data would be handled through Special Uncorrectable Error\nhandling.  L1 data and instruction caches also have a retry capability\nfor intermittent errors and a cache set delete mechanism for handling\nsolid failures.\nSpecial Uncorrectable Error handling\nSpecial Uncorrectable Error (SUE) handling prevents an\nuncorrectable error in memory or modified cache data from immediately\ncausing the system to terminate.  Rather, the system tags the data and\ndetermines whether it will ever be used again.  If the error is\nirrelevant, it will not force a check stop.  When and if data is used,\nI/O adapters controlled by an I/O hub controller would freeze if data\nwere transferred to an I/O device, otherwise, termination may be\nlimited to the program/kernel or if the data is not owned by the\nhypervisor.\nPCI extended error handling\nPCI extended error handling (EEH)-enabled adapters respond to a\nspecial data packet generated from the affected PCI slot hardware by\ncalling system firmware, which will examine the affected bus, allow\nthe device driver to reset it, and continue without a system reboot.\nFor Linux, EEH support extends to the majority of frequently used\ndevices, although some third-party PCI devices may not provide native\nEEH support.\nUncorrectable error recovery\nWhen the auto-restart option is enabled, the system can\nautomatically restart following an unrecoverable software error,\nhardware failure, or environmentally induced (AC power) failure.\nServiceability\nThe purpose of serviceability is to efficiently repair the system\nwhile attempting to minimize or eliminate impact to system operation.\nServiceability includes system installation, MES (system\nupgrades/downgrades), and system maintenance/repair.  Depending upon\nthe system and warranty contract, service may be performed by the\nclient, an IBM representative, or an authorized warranty service\nprovider.\nThe serviceability features delivered in this system help provide a\nhighly efficient service environment by incorporating the following\nattributes:\nDesign for SSR Setup, Install, and Service\nError Detection and Fault Isolation (ED/FI)\nFirst Failure Data Capture (FFDC)\nGuiding Light service indicators\nService labels and service diagrams available on the system and\ndelivered through IBM Knowledge Center\nStep-by-step service procedures documented in IBM Knowledge Center\nor available through the HMC\nAutomatic reporting of serviceable events to IBM through the\nElectronic Service Agent Call Home application\nService environment\nIn the PowerVM environment, the HMC is a dedicated server that\nprovides functions for configuring and managing servers for either\npartitioned or full-system partition using a GUI or command-line\ninterface (CLI) or REST API.  An HMC attached to the system enables\nsupport personnel (with client authorization) to remotely, or locally\nto the physical HMC that is in proximity of the server being serviced,\nlog in to review error logs and perform remote maintenance if\nrequired.\nThe POWER9 processor-based platforms support several service\nenvironments:\nAttachment to one or more HMCs or vHMCs is a supported option by\nthe system with PowerVM.  This is the default configuration for\nservers supporting logical partitions with dedicated or virtual I/O.\nIn this case, all servers have at least one logical partition.\nService interface\nSupport personnel can use the service interface to communicate with\nthe service support applications in a server using an operator\nconsole, a graphical user interface on the management console or\nservice processor, or an operating system terminal.  The service\ninterface helps to deliver a clear, concise view of available service\napplications, helping the support team to manage system resources and\nservice information in an efficient and effective way.  Applications\navailable through the service interface are carefully configured and\nplaced to give service providers access to important service\nfunctions.\nDifferent service interfaces are used, depending on the state of\nthe system, hypervisor, and operating environment.  The primary\nservice interfaces are:\nLEDs\nOperator Panel\nService Processor menu\nOperating system service menu\nService Focal Point on the HMC or vHMC with PowerVM\nIn the guiding light LED implementation, the system can clearly\nidentify components for replacement by using specific component-level\nLEDs . The servicer can use the identify function to blink the\nFRU-level LED.  When this function is activated, a roll-up to the blue\nenclosure locate and system locate LEDs will occur.  These enclosure\nLEDs will turn on solid and can be used to follow the light path from\nthe system to the enclosure and down to the specific FRU in the\nPowerVM environment.\nFirst Failure Data Capture and error data analysis\nFirst Failure Data Capture (FFDC) is a technique that helps ensure\nthat when a fault is detected in a system, the root cause of the fault\nwill be captured without the need to re-create the problem or run any\nsort of extending tracing or diagnostics program.  For the vast\nmajority of faults, a good FFDC design means that the root cause can\nalso be detected automatically without servicer intervention.\nFFDC information, error data analysis, and fault isolation are\nnecessary to implement the advanced serviceability techniques that\nenable efficient service of the systems and to help determine the\nfailing items.\nIn the rare absence of FFDC and Error Data Analysis, diagnostics\nare required to re-create the failure and determine the failing items.\nDiagnostics\nGeneral diagnostic objectives are to detect and identify problems\nso they can be resolved quickly.  Elements of IBM's diagnostics\nstrategy include:\nProvide a common error code format equivalent to a system\nreference code with PowerVM, system reference number, checkpoint, or\nfirmware error code.\nProvide fault detection and problem isolation procedures.  Support\nremote connection ability to be used by the IBM Remote Support Center\nor IBM Designated Service.\nProvide interactive intelligence within the diagnostics with\ndetailed online failure information while connected to IBM's back-end\nsystem.\nAutomatic diagnostics\nThe processor and memory FFDC technology is designed to perform\nwithout the need for re-create diagnostics nor require user\nintervention.  Solid and intermittent errors are designed to be\ncorrectly detected and isolated at the time the failure occurs.\nRuntime and boot-time diagnostics fall into this category.\nStand-alone diagnostics with PowerVM\nAs the name implies, stand-alone or user-initiated diagnostics\nrequires user intervention.  The user must perform manual steps,\nincluding:\nBooting from the diagnostics CD, DVD, USB, or network\nInteractively selecting steps from a list of choices\nConcurrent maintenance\nThe determination of whether a firmware release can be updated\nconcurrently is identified in the readme information file that is\nreleased with the firmware.  An HMC is required for the concurrent\nfirmware update with PowerVM.  In addition, concurrent maintenance of\nPCIe adapters is supported with PowerVM.  Concurrent maintenance of\nthe Operator Panel is supported through ASMI.  Additional concurrent\nmaintenance includes:\nEXP24S SAS Storage enclosure drawer.\nDrives in the EXP24S Storage enclosure drawer.\nNVMe U.2 drives.\nPCI extender cards, Optical PCIe Link IO Expansion Card.\nPCIe I/O adapters.\nPCIe I/O drawers.\nPCIe to USB Conversion card.\nSMP cables.  (only after Nov GA and with Firmware 920.20)\nSystem node AC power supplies:  Two functional power supplies must\nremain installed at all times while the system is operating.\nSystem node fans.\nSystem control unit fans.\nSystem control unit Op Panel.\nTime of Day battery.\nUPIC Interface card in SCU.\nUPIC power cables from system node to system control unit.\nService labels\nService providers use these labels to assist them in performing\nmaintenance actions.  Service labels are found in various formats and\npositions and are intended to transmit readily available information\nto the servicer during the repair process.  Following are some of\nthese service labels and their purpose:\nLocation diagrams:  Location diagrams are located on the system\nhardware, relating information regarding the placement of hardware\ncomponents.  Location diagrams may include location codes, drawings of\nphysical locations, concurrent maintenance status, or other data\npertinent to a repair.  Location diagrams are especially useful when\nmultiple components such as DIMMs, CPUs, processor books, fans,\nadapter cards, LEDs, and power supplies are installed.\nRemove/replace procedures:  Service labels that contain\nremove/replace procedures are often found on a cover of the system or\nin other spots accessible to the servicer.  These labels provide\nsystematic procedures, including diagrams detailing how to remove or\nreplace certain serviceable hardware components.\nArrows:  Numbered arrows are used to indicate the order of\noperation and the serviceability direction of components.  Some\nserviceable parts such as latches, levers, and touch points need to be\npulled or pushed in a certain direction and in a certain order for the\nmechanical mechanisms to engage or disengage.  Arrows generally\nimprove the ease of serviceability.\nQR labels\nQR labels are placed on the system to provide access to key service\nfunctions through a mobile device.  When the QR label is scanned, it\nwill go to a landing page specific to that server which contains many\nof the service functions of interest while physically located at the\nserver.  These include things such as installation and repair\ninstructions, service diagrams, reference code look up, and so on.\nPackaging for service\nThe following service enhancements are included in the physical\npackaging of the systems to facilitate service:\nColor coding (touch points):  Blue-colored touch points delineate\ntouchpoints on service components where the component can be safely\nhandled for service actions such as removal or installation.\nTool-less design:  Selected IBM systems support tool-less or\nsimple tool designs.  These designs require no tools or simple tools\nsuch as flathead screw drivers to service the hardware components.\nPositive retention:  Positive retention mechanisms help to assure\nproper connections between hardware components such as cables to\nconnectors, and between two cards that attach to each other.  Without\npositive retention, hardware components run the risk of becoming loose\nduring shipping or installation, preventing a good electrical\nconnection.  Positive retention mechanisms like latches, levers,\nthumb-screws, pop Nylatches (U-clips), and cables are included to help\nprevent loose connections and aid in installing (seating) parts\ncorrectly.  These positive retention items do not require tools.\nError handling and reporting\nIn the event of system hardware or environmentally induced failure,\nthe system runtime error capture capability systematically analyzes\nthe hardware error signature to determine the cause of failure.  The\nanalysis result will be stored in system NVRAM.  When the system can\nbe successfully restarted either manually or automatically, or if the\nsystem continues to operate, the error will be reported to the\noperating system.  Hardware and software failures are recorded in the\nsystem log.  When an HMC is attached in the PowerVM environment, an\nELA routine analyzes the error, forwards the event to the Service\nFocal Point (SFP) application running on the HMC, and notifies the\nsystem administrator that it has isolated a likely cause of the system\nproblem.  The service processor event log also records unrecoverable\ncheckstop conditions, forwards them to the SFP application, and\nnotifies the system administrator.\nThe system has the ability to call home through the IBM i operating\nsystem to report platform-recoverable errors and errors associated\nwith PCI adapters/devices.\nIn the HMC-managed environment, a call home service request will be\ninitiated from the HMC and the pertinent failure data with service\nparts information and part locations will be sent to an IBM service\norganization.  Client contact information and specific system-related\ndata such as the machine type, model, and serial number, along with\nerror log data related to the failure, are sent to IBM Service.\nLive Partition Mobility\nWith PowerVM Live Partition Mobility (LPM), users can migrate an\nAIX, IBM i or Linux VM running on one POWER system to another POWER\nsystem without disrupting services.  The migration transfers the\nentire system environment, including processor state, memory, attached\nvirtual devices, and connected users.  It provides continuous\noperating system and application availability during planned outages\nfor repair of hardware and firmware faults.  The IBM Power System E980\nand other servers using POWER9-technology processors with firmware\nlevel FW920 or above supports secure LPM, whereby the VM image is\nencrypted and compressed prior to transfer.  Secure LPM uses on-chip\nencryption and compression capabilities of the POWER9 processor for\noptimal performance.\nService processor\nDiagnostic monitoring of recoverable error from the processor\nchipset is performed on the system processor itself, while the fatal\ndiagnostic monitoring of the processor chipset is performed by the\nservice processor.  It runs on its own boundary and does not require\nresources from a system processor to be operational to perform its\ntasks.\nUnder PowerVM, the service processor supports surveillance of the\nconnection to the HMC and to the system firmware (hypervisor).  It\nalso provides several remote power control options, environmental\nmonitoring, reset, restart, remote maintenance, and diagnostic\nfunctions, including console mirroring.  The service processors menus\n(ASMI) can be accessed concurrently with system operation, allowing\nnondisruptive abilities to change system default parameters.\nCall home\nCall home\nrefers to an automatic or manual call from a\nclient location to the IBM support structure with error log data,\nserver status, or other service-related information.  Call home\ninvokes the service organization in order for the appropriate service\naction to begin.  Call home can be done through HMC if the system i OS\nis running, it can also be configured to report OS detected errors.\nCall Home on the HMC will continue to report platform errors.  While\nconfiguring call home is optional, clients are encouraged to implement\nthis feature in order to obtain service enhancements such as reduced\nproblem determination and faster and potentially more accurate\ntransmittal of error information.  In general, using the call home\nfeature can result in increased system availability.  The Electronic\nService Agent application can be configured for automated call home.\nSee the next section for specific details on this application.\nIBM Electronic Services\nElectronic Service Agent and the IBM Electronic Services web portal\ncomprise the IBM Electronic Services solution, which is dedicated to\nproviding fast, exceptional support to IBM clients.  IBM Electronic\nService Agent is a no-charge tool that proactively monitors and\nreports hardware events such as system errors, performance issues, and\ninventory.  Electronic Service Agent can help focus on the client's\ncompany business initiatives, save time, and spend less effort\nmanaging day-to-day IT maintenance issues.\nSystem configuration and inventory information collected by\nElectronic Service Agent also can be viewed on the secure Electronic\nServices web portal and used to improve problem determination and\nresolution between the client and the IBM support team.  As part of an\nincreased focus to provide even better service to IBM clients,\nElectronic Service Agent tool configuration and activation comes\nstandard with the system.  In support of this effort, a new HMC\nExternal Connectivity security whitepaper has been published, which\ndescribes data exchanges between the HMC and the IBM Service Delivery\nCenter (SDC) and the methods and protocols for this exchange.  To read\nthe whitepaper and prepare for Electronic Service Agent installation,\nsee the \"Security\" section at the\nIBM Electronic Service Agent\nwebsite.\nSelect your country.\nClick \"IBM Electronic Service Agent Connectivity Guide.\"\nBenefits:  increased uptime\nElectronic Service Agent is designed to enhance the warranty and\nmaintenance service by potentially providing faster hardware error\nreporting and uploading system information to IBM Support.  This can\noptimize the time monitoring the symptoms, diagnosing the error, and\nmanually calling IBM Support to open a problem record.  And 24x7\nmonitoring and reporting means no more dependency on human\nintervention or off-hours client personnel when errors are encountered\nin the middle of the night.\nSecurity:\nThe Electronic Service Agent tool is designed\nto help secure the monitoring, reporting, and storing of the data at\nIBM.  The Electronic Service Agent tool is designed to help securely\ntransmit either through the internet (HTTPS or VPN) or modem to\nprovide clients a single point of exit from their site.  Communication\nis one way.  Activating Electronic Service Agent does not enable IBM\nto call into a client's system.\nFor additional information, see the\nIBM Electronic Service Agent\nwebsite.\nMore accurate reporting\nBecause system information and error logs are automatically\nuploaded to the IBM Support Center in conjunction with the service\nrequest, clients are not required to find and send system information,\ndecreasing the risk of misreported or misdiagnosed errors.  Once\ninside IBM, problem error data is run through a data knowledge\nmanagement system, and knowledge articles are appended to the problem\nrecord.\nCustomized support\nBy using the IBMid entered during activation, clients can view\nsystem and support information in the \"My Systems\" and \"Premium\nSearch\" sections of the Electronic Services website.\nThe Electronic Services web portal is a single internet entry point\nthat replaces the multiple entry points traditionally used to access\nIBM internet services and support.  This web portal enables you to\ngain easier access to IBM resources for assistance in resolving\ntechnical problems.  The newly improved My Systems and Premium Search\nfunctions make it even easier for Electronic Service Agent-enabled\nclients to track system inventory and find pertinent fixes.\nMy Systems provides valuable reports of installed hardware and\nsoftware using information collected from the systems by IBM\nElectronic Service Agent.  Reports are available for any system\nassociated with the client's IBMid.  Premium Search combines the\nfunction of search and the value of Electronic Service Agent\ninformation, providing advanced search of the technical support\nknowledgebase.  Using Premium Search and the Service Agent information\nthat has been collected from the system, clients are able to see\nsearch results that apply specifically to their systems.For more\ninformation on how to utilize the power of IBM Electronic Services,\nsee the following website or contact an\nIBM Systems Services Representative.\nIBM Proactive Support for Power Systems\nClients have found significant value in IBM's Proactive Support\nofferings on mission-critical systems, as this provides personalized\nsupport, proactive recommendations and accelerated response times vs.\nstandard support. Compared to a\nSAS or SATA SSD, the NVMe Flash adapter provides more read/write\ninput/output operations per second (IOPS) and larger throughput\n(GB/sec).\nCCIN is 58FD.\nFeature #EC5C and #EC5D are identical cards except that the\ntailstock bracket is different.  #EC5C fits a low profile PCIe slot.\n#EC5D fits a full high PCIe slot.  See also EC5E for a card with more\nmemory.\nThe nature of the workload has a great impact on the maximum write\ncapacity.  If a high percentage of more sequentially oriented writes\nare used instead of random writes, the maximum write capacity will be\nlarger.  To extend the life of the device, the application that is\nusing the device must convert small random writes to larger sequential\nwrites.  Writes past the adapter's maximum write capacity will\ncontinue to work for some period of time, but much more slowly.\nWhether the application uses sequential or random reads from the\ndevice does not affect the life of the device.  A Predictive Failure\nAnalysis message will indicate that it is time to replace the adapter\nif enabled by the system administrator.  Customers are recommended to\nmonitor the smart log via their operating system where fuel gauge\nshows the percentage used.\nIBM NVMe adapter failures will be replaced during the standard\nwarranty and maintenance period for adapters that have not reached the\nmaximum number of write cycles.  Adapters that reach this limit may\nfail to operate according to specifications and must be replaced at\nthe client's expense.  Data protection is not implemented in the card;\nprotection is provided by OS mirroring or software RAID wherever\napplicable.\nThis adapter is not supported in the PCIe I/O drawer.\nNote:\nNVMe Flash adapters #EC5C can be used to meet minimum AIX/Linux\nSSD/HDD and backplane requirements.\nThis PCIe NVMe device can have 32 namespaces per device.\nAttributes provided:  3.2 TB of low latency flash memory with boot\ncapability\nAttributes required:  PCIe slot in system unit\nMinimum required:  0\nMaximum allowed:  32 (Initial order maximum:  32)\nOS level required:\nAIX Version 7.2 with the 7200-03 Technology Level and Service Pack\n7200-03-03-1914, or later\nAIX Version 7.1 with the 7100-05 Technology Level and Service Pack\n7100-05-04-1914, or later\nAIX Version 7.2 with the 7200-01 Technology Level and Service Pack\n7200-01-06-1914, or later\nAIX Version 7.2 with the 7200-02 Technology Level and Service Pack\n7200-02-04-1914, or later\nAIX Version 7.1 with the 7100-04 Technology Level and Service Pack\n7100-04-08-1914, or later\nIBM i requires VIOS\nRed Hat Enterprise Linux 7 for Power LE, version 7.6, or later\nRed Hat Enterprise Linux 8.0 for Power LE, or later\nSUSE Linux Enterprise Server 12 Service Pack 4, or later\nInitial Order/MES/Both/Supported:  Both\nCSU:  Yes\nReturn parts MES:  No\nNote:\nAssignment to the VIOS requires VIOS 3.1.0.21, or later;\nVIOS 2.2.6.41, or later.\n(#EC5E) PCIe3 x8 LP 6.4 TB NVMe Flash adapter for AIX/Linux\n(No Longer Available as of May 12, 2023)\nThe PCIe3 x8 6.4 TB NVMe Adapter is a Peripheral Component\nInterconnect Express (PCIe) generation 3 (Gen3) x8 adapter. Also the drive was not tested\nwith 4096 byte sectors and thus JBOD mode for AIX/Linux is not\nsupported.  4k drives cannot be reformatted to 5xx drives (or vice\nversa).\nNote:\nAs part of a larger industry transition, IBM Power Systems is in\nthe process of gradually shifting away from offering 5xx (512/ 528)\nbyte sector SAS drives (HDD or SSD) to 4K byte sector drives.  Most\nAIX/Linux applications access SAS drives through a file system and\nexperience no effect of this sector size transition.  In much less\ncommon cases, an AIX/Linux application may access the disk drive\ndirectly through the raw device interface and may still require only\n5xx byte sectors drives.  If there are 4k usage concerns, check with\nthe application provider to ensure compatibility with 4K byte sector\ndrives.\nAttributes provided:  one 1.55 TB SFF-2 4k SSD\nAttributes required:  one SFF-2 SAS bay, PCIe3 SAS controller\nMinimum required:  0\nMaximum allowed:  2016 (Initial order maximum:  999)\nOS level required:\nIBM i supported\nInitial Order/MES/Both/Supported:  Both\nCSU:  Yes\nReturn parts MES:  No\n(#EU01) 1TB Removable Disk Drive Cartridge\n(No longer available as of January 12, 2024)\n1TB Removable Disk Drive Cartridge (#EU01) provides a RDX disk\ndrive in a rugged cartridge to be used in an RDX Internal and External\nDocking Station such as the (#1103, #1104 or #1123, #EU03, #EU04\n,#EU23, or #EU07 1TB is uncompressed.  docking station.  1TB is\nuncompressed.
